nameStory: The white mulberry gets its name from its pale, whitish berries, though they can actually range from white to pink to purple when ripe. The Latin name 'alba' literally means 'white,' referring to these light-colored fruits that distinguish it from its darker-fruited cousin, the red mulberry.
description: White mulberry is a fast-growing, medium-sized tree that reaches 30-65 feet tall with a broad, rounded crown. Originally from China, this naturalized tree has spread throughout New England, often appearing in disturbed areas and along roadsides. Its glossy, heart-shaped leaves can be quite variable - some smooth-edged, others deeply lobed, sometimes even on the same tree. The small, clustered berries look like tiny blackberries and are edible, though somewhat bland compared to other wild fruits.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Glossy, bright green leaves that feel smooth and slightly waxy to the touch, arranged alternately on branches. Shape varies dramatically - some are simple ovals, others have deep lobes like mittens, often mixed on the same tree.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small aggregate berries about half an inch long that look like tiny mulberries, starting white or pale pink and sometimes darkening to purple. They're sweet but rather bland, with a slightly gritty texture from tiny seeds.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Grayish-brown bark that becomes furrowed and ridged with age on mature trees. Younger branches are smooth with a slight orange tint when scratched.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Fast-growing tree with a broad, spreading crown and somewhat irregular branching pattern. Often multi-trunked or with low, spreading branches.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous flowers appear in spring in small, catkin-like clusters. Male and female flowers are usually on separate trees, with males producing abundant pollen in drooping clusters.

habitat: White mulberry thrives in disturbed soils and sunny locations throughout New England, commonly found along roadsides, in old fields, and at forest edges. It's particularly abundant in urban and suburban areas where it readily colonizes vacant lots and disturbed ground. This adaptable tree tolerates poor soils and pollution better than many native species.

seasonality.spring: Small, greenish flower clusters appear in May before or with the emerging leaves. The glossy new leaves unfurl in various shapes, making this a good time to observe the remarkable leaf variation on a single tree.
seasonality.summer: Berries ripen from June through July, starting pale and sometimes darkening with age. The full canopy of glossy green leaves is most distinctive during this season.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn bright yellow before dropping, and any remaining fruits may persist briefly. Fall is when the leaf shape variation is most obvious as leaves prepare to drop.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches reveal the spreading growth habit and grayish, furrowed bark. Winter buds are small and reddish-brown, arranged alternately along the twigs.

funFact: White mulberry pollen is launched from the male flowers at over 350 miles per hour - more than half the speed of sound! This explosive pollen release happens so fast it's visible to the naked eye as tiny puffs shooting from the flowers, making it one of nature's speediest botanical launches.
confusionNotes: White mulberry is often confused with native red mulberry, but white mulberry leaves feel glossy and waxy (red mulberry leaves are rougher and sandpapery underneath), and white mulberry shows much more dramatic leaf shape variation on the same tree. Memory trick: 'White and waxy, wildly varied' - the smooth, glossy leaves in many different shapes are your giveaway.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, white mulberry fruits aren't always white - they can be pink or even purple when ripe. This non-native species was introduced to North America in colonial times to support silk production, as its leaves are the preferred food of silkworms. It has since naturalized widely and can hybridize with our native red mulberry.
compareHints: White mulberry differs from native red mulberry by its glossy, waxy-feeling leaves (versus red mulberry's rough, sandpapery leaf undersides) and more extreme leaf shape variation on individual trees. Red mulberry fruits are typically darker and more flavorful, while white mulberry fruits are often paler and blander, though color alone isn't reliable since both species can produce various colored fruits.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Korean mulberry is distinguished from white mulberry by its rougher, more sandpapery leaves and longer, more cylindrical fruits.
Red mulberry differs from white mulberry by its rougher, sandpaper-textured leaves and deeper-colored, more flavorful fruits.
